appraisal_events.evidence: Caught in her earlier oath — "Vous m'aviez juré, il n'y a pas un an, n'avoir rien fait aux Buttes-Chaumont" — she answers "J'avais peur de vous faire de la peine", and again "ma petite Andrée, vous mentez encore"; the narration anatomizes her "envie et orgueil", her rages in which she wished to dishonour people on false testimony, and reveals that she called the young man a wretch only because she was mad about him and thought he did not want her.
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage takes Andrée apart: a serial liar under oath, moved by envy and the need to humiliate before she can love, and suspected of confessing this time precisely in order to hurt.

appraisal_events.evidence: Andrée names the Buttes-Chaumont house, the trees, "la grotte du petit Trianon"; "l'Albertine réelle que je découvrais ... différait fort peu de la fille orgiaque surgie et devinée, le premier jour, sur la digue de Balbec"; her oath "sur la tombe de ma pauvre mère" is now worthless, and belief in her innocence has given way to belief in her guilt.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narration settles its verdict against Albertine: the first intuition of the orgiac girl is ratified, and the denials he had preferred to the evidence are judged to have been credulity on his part.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Je crois qu'elle a été forcée de vous quitter par sa tante"; Mme Bontemps was pressed by the suitor, Mme Verdurin was matchmaking for her nephew, and the note about the "sentiment si familial" turns out to concern him and not Mlle Vinteuil; "Ainsi Albertine ... avait eu, somme toute, un beau parti bourgeois", and "à mon avis elle avait été une victime".
appraisal_events.explanation: A second explanation reaches him in which Albertine is a courted match pressed by her family rather than a fugitive from surveillance, and her most incriminating blush becomes innocent; the passage neither confirms nor rejects it.

appraisal_events.evidence: The Balbec idler known as "la brute épaisse", expelled from school and living at baccarat and polo, has his sketches, sets and costumes staged: "les juges les plus autorisés considérèrent ses œuvres comme quelque chose de capital, presque des œuvres de génie, et je pense d'ailleurs comme eux"; the sceptics who credited the works to Andrée or to a hired professional are flatly wrong — "ce jeune homme était bien l'auteur de ces œuvres admirables."
appraisal_events.explanation: A distinct movement of the passage reverses everyone's estimate of Octave, with the most authorized judges and the narrator jointly crowning as genius the man the little band called a perfect fool.

status_effects.explanation: She is convicted of lying under oath, twice, and the narration credits her deepest working motives to envy, pride and the wish to humiliate.
The passage's verdict on her closes negatively: the orgiac girl of the first day is declared the real one, and her sworn denials are now read as lies.

Reported standing rises: a rich nephew of the Verdurins wanted to marry her, Mme Verdurin was working for the match and receiving her in a salon that marked her, and her aunt held the marriage over her.
The dunce and dandy is affirmed to be the true author of works the narrator himself judges close to genius.

His standing visibly rises in the world of the passage: the performances make "une assez grande impression", the most authorized judges pronounce his work capital, and those who explained it away are refuted.

ambiguities: The passage cannot decide which woman lied — "Mais pourquoi croire que c'était plutôt elle qu'Andrée qui mentait ?" — and raises that Andrée may have invented or exaggerated her revelations "pour que je ne fusse pas heureux", so the verdict recorded against Albertine rests on testimony the text itself distrusts.

Andrée's oath that nothing passed between Albertine and Mlle Vinteuil's circle cuts directly against the suspicion that had organized the narrator's jealousy, leaving Albertine's departure without a settled cause.
